questions.question: When should you use a channel, mutex, WaitGroup, or context in Go?
questions.title: Choosing the right concurrency tool
questions.direct_answer: Use a channel to transfer values or ownership between goroutines, a mutex to protect shared state that must remain shared, a `WaitGroup` to wait for a known set of tasks, and `context.Context` to propagate cancellation or deadlines. These tools solve different problems and are often combined rather than treated as interchangeable alternatives.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to map communication, mutual exclusion, completion, and cancellation to distinct primitives.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a channel as a complicated lock or expecting context cancellation to wait for goroutines to finish.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe one design that deliberately combines cancellation, completion, and state ownership.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Channels transfer data, events, or ownership and can apply backpressure.
A mutex serializes access to shared memory; keep its protected region small.
A WaitGroup counts task completion but carries no result and cancels nothing.
Context broadcasts cancellation and deadlines but does not confirm shutdown.
Choose from the relationship you need, then combine tools when responsibilities differ.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
I choose a concurrency primitive from the relationship it must express. A channel transfers a value or event and can move ownership from producer to consumer. It is a good fit for pipelines, job queues, result streams, and select-based coordination. Capacity then defines where backpressure occurs.

A `sync.Mutex` is more direct when several goroutines truly share one piece of state, such as an in-memory cache or counter. Locking protects an invariant across a small group of reads and writes. I do not replace a simple critical section with a channel-owning goroutine unless serialized commands or lifecycle behaviour add real value.

A `sync.WaitGroup` answers only “have these tasks returned?” For example, after launching four workers, the owner can wait for all four. It does not collect their errors, limit their number, or tell them to stop. A context answers a different question: “is this operation canceled or past its deadline?” Cancellation is a signal, so the owner may still use a WaitGroup to confirm exit.

A server operation can combine all four: context cancels request work, a jobs channel distributes owned tasks, a mutex protects a small shared metric, and a WaitGroup joins workers during shutdown. Keeping each responsibility explicit, observable, and independently testable is much simpler than forcing one primitive to pretend it provides all four guarantees.

sections.title: Concept guide · Choosing the right concurrency tool
sections.content:
Concurrency becomes easier to reason about when each relationship has one name. Data flow asks who owns a value next. Shared state asks which operations must be atomic together. Completion asks which tasks the owner must join. Lifetime asks when work is no longer wanted. Channels, mutexes, WaitGroups, and contexts align with those questions.

The slogan about communicating instead of sharing memory is guidance, not a ban on locks. A mutex may be the clearest representation of a short shared invariant. Conversely, a channel is useful when the transfer, queue, or ordering is part of the behaviour. The design should minimize shared mutable ownership, not maximize use of any one syntax.

sections.title: One primary responsibility per tool
sections.content:
| Tool | Primary job | Does not provide by itself |
|---|---|---|
| Channel | Value/event transfer and backpressure | Automatic cancellation of producers |
| `sync.Mutex` | Exclusive access to shared state | Task completion or data transfer |
| `sync.WaitGroup` | Wait for registered tasks | Errors, results, or cancellation |
| `context.Context` | Propagate cancellation/deadline | Proof that goroutines have returned |
| Atomic operation | One small atomic state transition | Multi-field invariants or lifecycle |

questions.question: How do you design a bounded Go worker pool that shuts down cleanly?
questions.title: A bounded, owned, cancellable worker pool
questions.direct_answer: Create a fixed number of workers reading from a jobs channel, let one producer or coordinator close jobs, and track workers with a WaitGroup. Close results only after all workers finish. Pass a context through the pool and select it at blocking boundaries so cancellation stops job intake and result publication without leaked goroutines.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether worker count, channel ownership, close order, results, and cancellation form one coherent lifecycle.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Closing results while workers can still send, or returning on cancellation without unblocking the producer.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: State every owner and prove the shutdown order from producer through coordinator to consumer.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Worker count bounds active processing; queue capacity bounds waiting work.
The jobs producer owns closing jobs after its final send.
Workers never close their shared results channel.
A coordinator waits for every worker, then closes results exactly once.
Context must be checked where job receive, external work, or result send can block.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A worker pool starts a fixed number of goroutines instead of one goroutine per input. All workers receive from one jobs channel, so each job goes to one worker. The worker count is the active concurrency budget, while the channel capacity is only the waiting-queue budget. I choose both from CPU, connection, API, or memory limits.

Ownership defines shutdown. The code producing jobs closes the jobs channel after the last send. Workers range or receive until that stream ends, then return and call `Done` on a WaitGroup. Because several workers send results, none of them closes the shared output. A coordinator waits for all workers and closes results once.

For example, two workers can square four integers. Results may arrive in a different order, but the consumer can aggregate them until the results channel closes. The close proves there will be no late sends because it occurs only after the worker WaitGroup reaches zero.

In production I pass a context into the pool. The producer stops enqueueing after cancellation, each worker stops waiting or performing context-aware I/O, and result sends select cancellation in case the consumer leaves. Cancellation requests shutdown; the WaitGroup confirms it. Error policy must also be explicit—collect all errors or cancel on the first, but never abandon blocked participants or silently lose their final errors.

sections.title: Build shutdown as a dependency graph
sections.content:
A clean worker pool ends in the reverse order of its data dependencies. The producer finishes and closes jobs. That lets workers know no more input exists. Workers finish their current jobs, publish their last results, and return. Only then can the coordinator close results, allowing the consumer's range to end.

Cancellation adds alternate edges to this graph. Any component blocked on a channel operation must be able to observe that the operation is no longer needed. A context-aware select provides that exit, but the owner still needs to join started goroutines if their resource cleanup matters. This explicit order prevents send-on-closed panics, close-twice panics, and silent leaks.

sections.title: Worker-pool ownership and shutdown
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P[Producer owns jobs close] --> J[jobs channel]
  J --> W1[Worker 1]
  J --> W2[Worker 2]
  W1 --> R[results channel]
  W2 --> R
  W1 -- Done --> G[WaitGroup coordinator]
  W2 -- Done --> G
  G -- close after Wait --> R
  R --> C[Consumer ranges]
  X[Context cancel] -.-> P
  X -.-> W1
  X -.-> W2
```
